questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Meaning and Scope of Biotechnology' refers to.
questions.a: Biotechnology is the umbrella name for every technique that puts living cells, or molecules harvested from them, to work manufacturing items people need - from bread and curd to vaccines and transgenic crops.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Meaning and Scope of Biotechnology'.
questions.a: The word fuses biology with technology: life processes harnessed to make products of value.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Meaning and Scope of Biotechnology' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Chapter 1 opening (source: kebt101.txt chapter opening and section 1.1)

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Historical Phases of Biotechnology' refers to.
questions.a: The subject passes through three eras: a prehistoric phase of crop cultivation and animal domestication, a classical phase built on brewing and fermenting, and the present phase of gene-level engineering that began once DNA structure was solved.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Historical Phases of Biotechnology'.
questions.a: The toolkit evolved from picking better seeds to stitching DNA, while the aim of useful products stayed fixed.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Historical Phases of Biotechnology' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.1 (source: kebt101.txt section 1.1 Historical Perspectives)

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Fermentation in Traditional Food Processing' refers to.
questions.a: Fermentation is the microbe-driven, enzyme-guided chemical change of organic matter; dough left overnight or grape juice invaded by yeast turns into leavened bread and wine by accident, which is how several staple foods began.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Fermentation in Traditional Food Processing'.
questions.a: Lactobacillus in curd converts milk constituents so that lactic acid clots the milk protein into solid curds, leaving watery whey behind.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Fermentation in Traditional Food Processing' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.1 (source: kebt101.txt section 1.1 and Box 1 (curd making))

Take the relation taught for 'Compound Microscope Magnification' and work with: eyepiece_mag = 360, object_size = 1024, objective_mag = 12. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of apparent_size.
questions.a: 4423680 bytes

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Compound Microscope Magnification' refers to.
questions.a: A compound microscope enlarges in two stages: the objective lens forms a first enlarged image of the specimen and the eyepiece magnifies that image again, so the overall power equals the product of the two lens powers.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Compound Microscope Magnification'.
questions.a: Multiply the two lens powers; a 10x eyepiece with a 40x objective shows the object 400 times larger.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Compound Microscope Magnification', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: total_power = eyepiece_mag * objective_mag

concepts.title: Fermented Share of the World Diet

questions.q: Using the method 'Fermented Share of the World Diet', work with: food_each = 50, people = 1200. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of fermented_part.
questions.a: 20000 units

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Fermented Share of the World Diet' and work with: food_each = 30, people = 2500. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of fermented_part.
questions.a: 25000 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Fermented Share of the World Diet' refers to.
questions.a: Close to one third of everything humans eat worldwide is fermented, so the fermented tonnage for any population can be estimated as its total food intake divided by three.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Fermented Share of the World Diet'.
questions.a: Scale any food total by the factor one third to get its fermented component.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Fermented Share of the World Diet', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: fermented_part = total_food / 3

concepts.title: Bt Cotton Share of the Hybrid Seed Market

questions.q: Using the method 'Bt Cotton Share of the Hybrid Seed Market', work with: seed_market = 24. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of non_bt_value.
questions.a: 13.2 units

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Bt Cotton Share of the Hybrid Seed Market' and work with: seed_market = 5. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of non_bt_value.
questions.a: 2.75 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Bt Cotton Share of the Hybrid Seed Market' refers to.
questions.a: Cotton engineered with the insect-killing Cry protein made by the soil bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis leads Indian hybrid seed sales, holding roughly 45 percent of that market by value.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Bt Cotton Share of the Hybrid Seed Market'.
questions.a: A percent share of a market means market total times 45 divided by 100; the remainder is the total minus that share.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Bt Cotton Share of the Hybrid Seed Market', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: bt_value = seed_market * 45 / 100

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Colour-Coded Branches of Biotechnology' refers to.
questions.a: Applications are labelled by colour: red covers medical products such as insulin, enzymes, antibiotics and vaccines; green covers eco-friendly plant work including transgenic crops; blue covers marine and freshwater organisms; white covers industrial processes with enzymes as green catalysts.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Colour-Coded Branches of Biotechnology'.
questions.a: Four colours sort the field: red heals, green feeds, blue explores water, white builds industry.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Colour-Coded Branches of Biotechnology' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.1 Table 1.1 (source: kebt101.txt Table 1.1)

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Application Domains of Modern Biotechnology' refers to.
questions.a: Gene-cutting technology now serves four headline areas - healing (recombinant insulin, growth hormone, gene therapy for ADA-SCID, genetic tests for phenylketonuria), farming (Bt crops, herbicide-tolerant soybean, Flavr Savr tomato, Golden Rice), food processing (industrial fermented foods) and planet care (bioremediation of pollutants and hyper-accumulator plants that soak up heavy metals).

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Application Domains of Modern Biotechnology'.
questions.a: One toolkit, four arenas: the same recombinant DNA logic heals patients, upgrades crops, improves food and cleans polluted sites.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Application Domains of Modern Biotechnology' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.2 (source: kebt101.txt sections 1.2 to 1.3.2)
